# Deployment-at-Scale Principles {.unnumbered}

Parts I and II built the fleet, coordinated its distributed state, and executed the training run. But training a model is only the opening chapter of its lifecycle; production deployment is the true test of operational accountability. Part III shifts the focus from the single, massive training run orchestrated across a dedicated cluster to the deployed fleet: the thousands of geographically distributed servers that answer requests in real time, the billions of edge devices that run and adapt models locally, and the operational machinery that keeps every deployed version accountable. The transition changes the engineering constraints. A training run must finish a coordinated workload; a deployed fleet must sustain useful throughput on a dynamic request stream while meeting latency targets, keep models current as data and devices change, and govern how each change reaches production.

A serving fleet depends on the runtime behavior of each replica: its execution time and memory footprint determine how many requests it can accept and how much capacity the fleet must provision. Part III therefore begins with performance engineering, revisiting the roofline model (@sec-appdx-dam-taxonomy), precision choices, and kernel execution to explain their consequences for fleet capacity and latency. Inference at scale uses that runtime foundation to coordinate request queues, batching, and distributed model state. Edge intelligence extends the argument to heterogeneous fleets with intermittent connectivity, including federated learning that coordinates training while data remains on participating devices. Production operations then governs rollout, monitoring, and recovery across the deployed fleet.

The principles below preview the serving constraints that performance engineering and inference at scale make quantitative; edge adaptation and fleet operations bring constraints of their own, which their chapters develop. Autoregressive generation produces each new token from the preceding tokens; a key-value cache retains intermediate attention state so the system can reuse it. A serving replica is one deployed copy of the model, potentially spread across devices. The chapters turn these concepts into capacity and latency models rather than assuming that local efficiency alone guarantees an efficient fleet.

The first constraint is imposed by the mechanics of generation itself.

::: {#pri-autoregressive-bottleneck .callout-principle title="The autoregressive bottleneck"}

**Invariant**: In low-batch dense transformer decode, weight streaming often makes throughput memory-bandwidth bound because every decode step must stream the model weights from device memory to the compute units. Higher batch sizes amortize weight streaming, and key-value (KV) cache traffic shifts the binding constraint at long context.

**Implication**: Throughput initially improves with batch size by amortizing weight reads across requests, until per-device latency budgets, KV cache capacity, or sustained compute become the binding ceiling. Serving systems therefore need batching, cache-management, and memory-layout policies that keep bandwidth useful without violating latency SLOs.

:::

The same accounting extends from device bandwidth to fleet economics.

::: {#pri-serving-cost-dominance .callout-principle title="The serving cost dominance law"}

**Invariant**: For high-traffic production models, cumulative inference cost can exceed the one-time training cost over the model's lifetime.

**Implication**: Inference efficiency often becomes the dominant lifecycle optimization target. Optimization efforts (quantization, distillation, sparsity) should be focused on the inference path when traffic volume, product lifetime, and retraining cadence make serving cost dominate.

:::

At scale, routing policy becomes another lever for protecting latency.

::: {#pri-power-two-choices .callout-principle title="The power of two choices (P2C)"}

**Invariant**: In the idealized process that sequentially places $R$ independent requests into $R$ replicas, with each request sampling replicas independently and uniformly at random, querying two replicas and selecting the least-loaded one reduces the maximum load from the one-choice bound $\Theta(\log R / \log \log R)$ to $\Theta(\log \log R)$ with high probability.

**Implication**: Simple randomized load-balancing algorithms produce dramatically lower maximum-load bounds with $\mathcal{O}(1)$ coordination overhead. Under serving queueing assumptions, the lower maximum load translates into reduced tail latency at scale.

:::

Part III takes the trained model from the cluster to the world. The path begins with performance engineering, which diagnoses where a replica's time goes before choosing among precision, kernel, and compilation changes, and so determines how much of the hardware's theoretical capacity the system can actually use. It then moves to inference at scale, where request batching, cache management, routing, and sharding turn single-device efficiency into fleet-level latency control. Edge intelligence extends this discipline to phone-class devices that adapt models locally and coordinate through federated learning under unequal memory, power, and connectivity budgets, while operations at scale closes the loop by monitoring the deployed fleet, coordinating platform ownership, and responding when production behavior diverges from design assumptions. Measured against the Fleet Law, these chapters shift from the training step to the serving request. Performance engineering shrinks the per-replica compute term and exposes the memory traffic hidden inside it, inference at scale trades batching against the queueing and routing delays that play the role of $T_{\text{sync}}$, edge intelligence faces communication costs set by intermittent wireless links rather than a data-center fabric, and operations bounds the coordination cost of every rollout and rollback. Together, these chapters develop the operational discipline that turns a trained model into a durable production system.
